title: What did you do yesterday?
goal: Talk about things that have happened using the *Perfekt* — the only past tense Germans use in everyday conversation.
bekal: form the Partizip II of regular and irregular verbs
build past-tense sentences with *haben* + Partizip II
tell people about your own weekend

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Montagmorgen
dialogs.intro: Monday morning in class. Frau Weber's first question is always the same, and the answers always have the same shape: *haben* in second position, the main verb at the end.

lines.speaker: Frau Weber:
lines.text: Guten Morgen! Was haben Sie am Wochenende gemacht?
lines.id: Good morning! What did you do at the weekend?
lines.literal: good morning! what have you at-the weekend made?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ich habe am Samstag Fußball gespielt.
lines.literal: I have on Saturday soccer played.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Danach habe ich geduscht und ein bisschen geschlafen.
lines.id: After that I took a shower and slept a bit.
lines.literal: after-that have I showered and a bit slept.

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Ich habe am Samstag gearbeitet. Zwölf Stunden!
lines.id: I worked on Saturday. Twelve hours!
lines.literal: I have on Saturday worked. twelve hours!

lines.speaker: Frau Weber:
lines.text: Zwölf Stunden? Haben Sie wenigstens gut gegessen?
lines.id: Twelve hours? Did you at least eat well?
lines.literal: twelve hours? have you at-least well eaten?

lines.speaker: Marek:
lines.text: Nein. Ich habe nur einen Kaffee getrunken.
lines.id: No. I only had a coffee.
lines.literal: no. I have only a coffee drunk.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Ich habe das ganze Wochenende gelesen. Zwei Bücher!
lines.id: I read all weekend. Two books!
lines.literal: I have the whole weekend read. two books!

lines.speaker: Frau Weber:
lines.text: Zwei Bücher! Und was haben Sie am Sonntag gemacht, Budi?
lines.id: Two books! And what did you do on Sunday, Budi?
lines.literal: two books! and what have you on Sunday made, Budi?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ich habe meinen Onkel besucht und wir haben zusammen gekocht.
lines.id: I visited my uncle and we cooked together.
lines.literal: I have my uncle visited and we have together cooked.

lines.speaker: Frau Weber:
lines.text: Und haben Sie auch Deutsch gelernt?
lines.id: And did you study German as well?
lines.literal: and have you also German learned?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ähm… Ich habe die Hausaufgaben vergessen. Tut mir leid!
lines.id: Um… I forgot the homework. Sorry!
lines.literal: um… I have the homework forgotten. makes me sorry!

notes: **Perfekt = *haben* in second position + Partizip II at the end.** A German past-tense sentence is always a bracket, exactly like the modal-verb sentences in unit 11: *Ich **habe** am Samstag Fußball **gespielt**.* Only *haben* changes form; the Partizip II never changes at all.

**Unlike English, spoken German hardly uses the simple past.** There is a *Präteritum* (*ich spielte*, *ich machte*), but that's written language — newspapers, novels, fairy tales. When you tell a story out loud, use the *Perfekt*, always. So *Ich habe gespielt* covers both "I played" and "I have played".

**Two exceptions you'll use every day:** *sein* and *haben* appear more often in their Präteritum form, ***war*** and ***hatte***. *Ich **war** gestern zu Hause* sounds far more natural than *ich bin gewesen*, and *Ich **hatte** keine Zeit* is more common than *ich habe gehabt*.

**Line 4: *Danach habe ich geduscht*.** The sentence starts with an adverb, so *haben* stays in second position and the subject moves behind it. Every word-order rule you've put in place still applies — the Perfekt adds no new rules, it just fills the end of the sentence.
**Perfekt questions put *haben* first:** *Haben Sie gut gegessen?*, *Was hast du gemacht?* The Partizip II stays at the end, whatever happens at the front.

***besucht*** and ***vergessen*** (lines 10 and 12) don't take *ge-*. Verbs beginning with *be-*, *ver-*, *er-*, *ent-* never get it — their past form is the same as, or almost the same as, the basic form.

grammars.title: Forming the Partizip II
body: The Partizip II is a frozen form of the verb — it never changes with the subject. There are four patterns, and which one applies depends on the type of verb.
after: The last row is the most distinctive: *ge-* is slipped **into the middle** of the word, right between the prefix and the verb. *Ich habe gestern **eingekauft**.* It looks odd, but once you see the separable verb joining back together at the end of the sentence, the position of *ge-* makes sense.

⚠️ There's no way to guess whether a verb is regular or not — just like English (*walk → walked* but *drink → drunk*). There are about two hundred irregular verbs, and fewer than fifty are really common. The appendix at the back of this book lists all the ones that appear here.

The most efficient way to memorize: learn each one **together with its helper verb** in one breath — *trinken, hat getrunken*. Learning a Partizip II without its *hat* or *ist* means learning half the information.

grammars.title: Past-tense word order
body: Same as with modal verbs: two poles, with the rest of the sentence in between.
after: The form of *haben* follows the subject as usual: *ich habe*, *du hast*, *er hat*, *wir haben*, *ihr habt*, *sie/Sie haben*. If you know the table from unit 4, you've already mastered half of the Perfekt.
**Where *nicht* goes:** right before the Partizip II. *Ich habe das **nicht** verstanden.* Same rule as with modal verbs — *nicht* always leans on the verb part at the end.

sections.title: The thirty most common Partizip II forms

blocks.text: All the verbs in this table use *haben*. The ones that use *sein* are collected in the next unit — don't mix the two yet.

Notice *vergessen*: its Partizip II is **exactly the same** as its basic form. A few other verbs behave this way — *bekommen*, *beginnen* — and it always happens with irregular verbs that have an inseparable prefix.

blocks.title: Words that move a story along
items: **dann / danach** — then, after that. *Dann habe ich eingekauft.*
**am Ende / zum Schluss** — in the end, finally. *Zum Schluss habe ich ferngesehen.*

blocks.text: Those four words turn a list of sentences into a story. And because they all stand in position one, they all push the subject behind *haben* — word-order practice that comes free with your past-tense practice.

items: Ich habe am Samstag Fußball gespielt.
Ich habe nur einen Kaffee getrunken.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right Partizip II.
Put the words in the right order to make a past-tense sentence.

answers: What did you do yesterday? — On Saturday I played soccer. — I only had a coffee. — We cooked together. — I forgot the homework. — It was great fun.
